Before you order lighted pine branches for your home, it's worth sitting with a few honest questions first.

I put this little buyer's guide together because product photos rarely tell you the things you actually need to know before you spend the money.

The photo running with this post is a side-by-side of the same room, taken from the same spot, at the same time of evening. The left side is labeled WITHOUT. The right side is labeled WITH. Nothing was rearranged between the two shots except one thing: the Enchanted Evergreen Pine from TwinklingTree, arranged in a plain vase and switched on.

The WITHOUT side isn't a bad room. It's clean, it's furnished, it's fine. It just reads a little flat once the sun goes down — the way most rooms do under overhead light. The WITH side is the same room with one soft point of warm golden light sitting on the table. That's the whole difference. And that's the honest scope of what this product does.

If you're deciding whether it belongs in your home, here is everything I'd want to know, laid out plainly.

1. How big is it, really?

Eighteen inches tall. That number matters more than any photo.

Eighteen inches means it's roughly the height of a table lamp without its shade. Tall enough to be noticed from across the room when it's lit. Small enough that it doesn't crowd a mantel, block a mirror, or take over a dining table.

If you were picturing a floor piece that fills a corner, this is not that. If you were picturing a little novelty trinket, it's not that either. It's an arrangement-sized piece — the scale you'd use for a vase of fresh branches from a florist.

A useful trick before you order: take a ruler or a rolled-up magazine, hold it at eighteen inches on the surface you're considering, and step back. If that height looks right in the spot, the scale will work.

2. What does it sit in?

Here's the part some listings gloss over, so I'll say it plainly: the vase is not included, and honestly, I think that's the right call.

These are loose Norfolk pine branches. You arrange them yourself in a vase you already own. I used a plain ceramic one from my own cabinet, and the arranging took maybe two minutes — set the branches in, spread them until they look natural, done.

Why does that matter? Because a vase packed in the box would match nobody's home. Your vase already matches your home. That's what keeps this from looking like a store display and starts making it look like something you put together yourself.

If you don't own a vase you like, a simple one from any home store will do. Heavier is better for stability. A wide mouth lets the branches fan out; a narrow one holds them more upright. Neither is wrong.

3. How bright is the glow — and will it keep you up at night?

This is decorative light, and I want to be direct about what that means.

The branches are threaded with small warm golden twinkles. Warm as in candlelight-colored, not the blue-white of a phone screen or an LED shop light. The glow is gentle enough to sit beside in the evening without it straining your eyes or dominating the room.

What it will not do is light your room. You will still turn on a lamp to read, still flip the switch when you cook. This is atmosphere, not illumination — the difference between a lit candle and a ceiling fixture. Any lighted branch sold as a lamp replacement is overpromising. This one doesn't need to.

A related worry, for anyone sensitive to light in the evening: warm gold at this scale is the gentlest category of decorative lighting there is. It's the tone of a low candle, not a screen. And since you switch it on and off yourself, the glow is there when you want it and gone when you don't.

What the WITH side of the photo shows is what actually happens: the nearby surfaces pick up a warm cast, the room gains a focal point after dark, and the space reads finished instead of flat. That's the honest job, and it does that job well.

4. Does it need an outlet?

No. It's battery powered, and that changes more than you'd expect.

Most of the best spots for a glow like this are exactly the spots with no outlet nearby — the middle of a mantel, the center of a dining table, an entryway console against a wall with nothing behind it. A corded piece forces you to decorate around the cord: hiding it behind books, taping it to the wall, or giving up on the spot altogether.

Cordless means you place it where it looks best, not where the wiring allows. It also means no white wire trailing down your mantel in the daytime, which is usually what gives away lighted decor before the lights even come on.

One practical note, because a buyer's guide should include it: batteries are batteries. You'll replace them from time to time, the same as a wall clock or a flameless candle. If you're the type who resents changing batteries in anything, weigh that honestly. For most people it's a fair trade for putting light in places lamps can't go.

5. Where does it actually work?

TwinklingTree suggests three placements on the official page, and they're the right three to consider.

The mantel. Eighteen inches is a comfortable mantel height — present without brushing the artwork or mirror above. If your mantel feels bare on one end, this fills it without a full styling project.

The table. On a dining table or side table, it works as a centerpiece you don't have to water, replace, or fuss over. On a smaller table beside a reading chair, it becomes the thing you switch on when you sit down for the evening.

The entryway. This might be the placement I'd argue for first. An entry console is the first surface you see coming home and the last one you pass at night. A soft golden glow there greets you at the door — and because it's cordless, an outlet-free entry table is no obstacle.

One piece, one spot, is the honest starting point. You don't need to buy three to find out whether you like it. Put it where you spend your evenings and see how the room feels after dark.

If you're torn between two spots, start where you sit longest after dinner. Decor earns its keep in the room where your evening actually happens — and at this size, it's easy to move if you change your mind.

6. Is it just a Christmas decoration?

Fair question, since pine is right there in the name.

Here's the distinction: Norfolk pine branches are a soft, graceful evergreen — closer to what a florist would put in a year-round arrangement than to a stiff Christmas-tree bough. There are no ornaments, no ribbon, no red-and-green anything. Greenery in a vase is a year-round look; it's the trimmings that make something read as December.

In November and December, it fits the season naturally. But in March, it's simply an evergreen arrangement with warm light in it — the way eucalyptus stems belong in any month. And the glow is golden, not multicolored, which matters more than people expect. Colored lights say holiday. Warm gold says evening.

If you'd feel obligated to box it up on January 2nd, you'd be boxing up a piece with nothing seasonal about it except the word pine. Mine stays out. It earns its place in July the same way it earns it in December: the room feels warmer after sunset with it than without it.

7. Will it look cheap up close?

This is the worry that stops most people, and it's a reasonable one, because plenty of lighted decor does look cheap — plastic-shiny needles, visible wire, lights so dense the greenery disappears.

A few things work in this piece's favor. Norfolk pine has naturally soft, feathery branching, an easier shape to render convincingly than stiff spruce. The twinkles are small and warm rather than large and glaring, so the light reads as glow, not bulbs. And because you arrange the branches yourself, they don't sit in the frozen, symmetrical pose that makes faux greenery look faux. Loose branches settled into your own vase carry the slight irregularity of a real arrangement — because it is one. You made it.

I'd also add: evening is when this piece does its work. Lit at dusk, in your vase, on your table, what registers is warm light through greenery. Nobody is inspecting needles by flashlight. And if you get it home and disagree, that's exactly what the guarantee below is for.

What it won't do

A fair guide includes the other column, so here it is.

It won't light your room. Covered above, but worth repeating: decorative glow, not functional lighting.

It won't fill a large empty corner. Eighteen inches is tabletop scale. If you need a six-foot statement piece, this isn't it.

It's indoor decor. It isn't made for a porch or patio.

It doesn't come with a vase. If you don't own one and don't want one, the branches will have nothing to stand in.

And it won't transform a room you dislike into a room you love. It does one thing: adds a warm, living-looking point of light to a surface after dark. As the photo shows, that one thing changes how a room feels in the evening. But it's an accent, and I'd rather you buy it as an accent than expect a renovation.

How much fussing does it take?

Some decor asks a lot of you. This asks for about two minutes, once.

You choose the vase. You set the branches in. You spread them until the shape pleases you — there is no wrong answer, since real arrangements aren't symmetrical either. Then you turn the lights on when you want them and off when you don't.

There's no watering, no wilting, no dropped needles to vacuum, no swapping stems when the season changes, no floral skills required. If you've ever put grocery-store flowers in water, you're overqualified.

That's worth naming, because plenty of us have quietly retired from decorating projects. Not from wanting a lovely home — from wanting one more thing to manage. This sits closer to a candle than a project: one small decision about placement, and then it simply does its evening job.

A quick way to decide

Here's the decision framework I'd offer a friend.

Skip it if: you want functional lighting, you need a large floor-standing piece, you want outdoor decor, or you'd resent ever changing a battery. None of those are what this is.

Consider it if: there's a surface in your home — a mantel end, an entry console, the table beside your chair — that looks fine by day and flat by night. That's the exact gap this fills. Look at your own room this evening after sunset and ask whether it resembles the WITHOUT photo. If it doesn't, you don't need this. If it does, you now know what the WITH version would look like, because the only variable between the two frames is this one piece, lit.

That's a more useful test than any adjective I could write.

The numbers, as of this writing

Price and terms change, so I'll date this: as of late August, the official TwinklingTree page shows the Enchanted Evergreen Pine at $39.99, marked down from $79.99 — a 50% reduction — with free shipping listed as a limited-time offer. Check the page for the current figures before you order; I'd rather you see today's terms than trust a Facebook post's memory.

One more thought about the price, since a guide should help you weigh it.

At $39.99 it sits in the range of a decent grocery-store bouquet and a half — except a bouquet is compost in ten days, and this is still on your mantel next year. If you're the sort who buys fresh flowers for the table, the math resolves quickly.

The guarantee, in plain terms

The official page states a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Here's why that matters more for this product than for most. The single thing no photo can settle — including the honest one above this post — is how the piece looks in your room, in your vase, at your dusk. Thirty days covers roughly thirty evenings of finding out.

Arrange it, place it, live with it through a few ordinary nights. If the glow doesn't earn its spot on your mantel or your entry table, send it back within the window for your money back. That converts this from a leap of faith into a home trial, which is the only way decor should be bought anyway.

I'd still read the guarantee terms on the product page before ordering — a careful buyer always does — but a stated 30-day money-back policy is why I'm comfortable saying: don't deliberate for three weeks. Deliberate at home, with the piece lit, where the question can actually be answered.

Where I landed

I'll close with the plain version of my own evening, since it's the most honest evidence I can offer.

I arranged the branches in a vase I already owned, set it on the entry console, and turned it on as the light outside was fading. Then I walked to the far side of the room and looked back — the same view the WITH photo shows.

The room hadn't changed. The furniture was the furniture; the walls were the walls. But the space had somewhere for the eye to rest — one warm golden point of it — and the whole room seemed to organize itself around that small glow, the way rooms organize themselves around a fireplace. It looked finished in a way it hadn't ten minutes earlier.

That's the entire promise, and I've tried to size it accurately: not a renovation, not a lamp, not a Christmas display. An 18-inch arrangement of graceful Norfolk pine with warm golden twinkles, standing in your own vase, in the one spot where your home goes flat after sunset.

If you've read this far and a particular surface came to mind, you already have your answer.

I'm 59 and I have been the first one awake in my house for thirty years. Now I keep a pair of sunglasses on the hook by my front door and I can have them on in four seconds. I got brushed off so badly by my dermatologist that I flew to France to get answers!

Let me explain, because I know how that sounds.

I'm 59, and I have been an early riser my whole life. Up at 5:40 without an alarm since my kids were small. Coffee at the kitchen window in the dark, watching the garden come up out of the grey. It's the best hour of my day and it has been for thirty years. I sleep seven and a half hours a night. People used to tell me I looked rested.

Then, about sixteen months ago, practically overnight, my under-eyes changed. Not gradually. All at once. Puffy and darker than ever, the skin gone thin and papery underneath. Like someone swapped out my face while I slept.

My eyes aged ten years in one winter. I am not exaggerating.

And my world started shrinking, one witness at a time.

First I stopped being in photos. Then I started sitting with my back to the window at lunch. Then I took the far chair at book club — the one in the dark corner. Until the only place my face existed in full daylight was my own kitchen, alone, before anyone else was up.

And even there, I wasn't safe. There is a pair of sunglasses hanging on the hook by my front door. They hang there permanently. They have one job. When the doorbell goes — a neighbour, a delivery, anyone — I can have them on in four seconds. I got that fast. I wear them on grey days. I have worn them indoors.

Fifty-nine years old, and I'd built myself a country with a border and one citizen.

So I paid to see a dermatologist. She looked at my face for about as long as it takes to read a menu and said, "Those are fat pads. It's the age. Everyone gets them."

I asked what could be done about them. She said, "Lower blepharoplasty," and wrote a number on the corner of a sheet of paper. Four figures, and it didn't start with a one.

Then she added the rest, the way you'd read a label. Cut the salt. Cut the evening wine. Sleep with your head elevated. And get more sleep — "you're clearly not getting enough." I told her I've slept seven and a half hours a night my whole life. She wrote down poor sleep hygiene anyway.

I said it happened in a few months. I'd had this same face for fifty-eight years. Age doesn't work on a deadline.

She shrugged. "It catches up with you." Appointment over. Fourteen minutes, and she still charged me for the consultation.

Do you understand what she did in that room? She didn't just dismiss me. She convicted my own life. My sleep, my mornings, the one glass of wine with dinner. She sent me home believing I'd done this to myself, one ordinary night at a time — and that the only door out was a knife.

I didn't accept it. Because women my age — women OLDER than me — didn't have this. My sister is 64 and she looks rested. So it couldn't be fifty-nine years of age arriving all at once, on schedule, in one winter.

Something else had happened. And my dermatologist either didn't know or didn't care what it was.

========

I became an expert in things that don't work.

The department-store eye cream I'd used faithfully for eleven years. A hundred and ten a jar, three jars. It had always kept me looking rested. Then the same product I'd used before just stopped working, and nobody could tell me why.

The protocol. This is the part that stung. No salt, no wine, wedge pillow, and sleep in — because I "wasn't getting enough." So the treatment for my eyes was to give up my mornings. I did it. Four months lying in bed until eight o'clock, propped up like a woman with a broken rib. My eyes were identical. I'd traded the best hour of my day for nothing.

A red light mask, a hundred and eighty-nine of them. Forty nights. My skin looked a little brighter. The bags were unmoved. (I understand why now. It was doing one third of the job.)

Nearly six hundred on lymphatic facial massage. Six sessions at ninety-five. And here's the maddening part — it worked. For about a day and a half. Then everything came back. The therapist told me honestly it needs doing every single day to hold.

Full-coverage concealer, fifty-four a bottle, three bottles. I could still see the half moons through all of it. Makeup only made it worse — it settled into the crepe and drew a line exactly where I didn't want one.

Thirteen months. Nineteen different creams, patches, tools and protocols. Just under three thousand.

Every one promised to depuff, brighten, firm, restore. Every one failed.

What I didn't know then was that every month I spent on the surface, the fluid underneath was still sitting there — staining the skin a little darker — and the little pump nobody had told me about was going a little slacker.

I wasn't just wasting money. I was wasting time I might not get back.

========

Here's where I did the thing my husband still teases me about.

One night, deep in a forum at 1 a.m., I read a comment from a woman who said the French have treated under-eye puffiness as a drainage problem since the 1930s, and that a therapist there had told her more in twenty minutes than three doctors had in two years.

I had frequent flyer points sitting unused. I booked five nights in Nice.

I told my husband I was going to get an answer if I had to knock on every pharmacy door on that coast. He said, "You know how this sounds." I said, "Yes. And I'm going."

Because here's what nobody tells you about being dismissed: it doesn't make you give up. It makes you furious enough to get on a plane.

========

The first pharmacy was polite and sold me a cream.

The second pharmacy was polite and sold me a better cream.

At the third, an older pharmacist looked at my face for a long moment, shook her head, and said, "Madame, creams will not help what you are describing." Then she took my receipt, turned it over, and wrote a name on the back.

"Colette. She has done drainage for forty years. Thursday mornings she is at the covered market. Go early."

I still have that receipt.

========

Thursday morning, at a covered market between a cheese stall and a flower seller, a woman named Colette — mid-70s, with this quiet elegance — had a small table with a lamp and a mirror on it.

She sat me down and pressed her thumb gently into the skin under my eye. Then she counted out loud.

The dent stayed there. Four full seconds before it slowly filled back in.

Then she said, "When did this start?"

"Sixteen months ago," I said. "Fast. My dermatologist says they're fat pads. She says it's my age and my sleep. She made it sound like I did this to my—"

"May I see you in the light?"

She turned my chin towards the light and looked for a long moment. Then she said the sentence I got on a plane for.

"Age did not do this in one winter. Age is slow. This was fast. Madame, these are not fat pads — fat does not dent. This is trapped fluid your body has stopped draining. You have been blaming your own sleep for a crime it did not commit."

I stood there in a food market and felt my eyes fill. For sixteen months, every morning had come with a side of guilt.

========

Colette had done drainage work on that coast for 40 years, trained in the method developed there in the 1930s. She walked me around the corner to a café, ordered two coffees, and showed me before-and-after photos from her practice.

The before photos looked exactly like my eyes. The after photos looked like my eyes from two years ago.

She pulled a pen and a napkin towards her and drew a ring. "Around your eye is a small ring of muscle. Every time you blink, it squeezes. That squeeze is a pump — it pushes fluid out of the thinnest skin on your body and into the channels that carry it away. It has done that every day since you were born."

"When your oestrogen drops, two things happen at once. The muscle goes slack, like every other muscle does. And the channels slow down. So the pump stops pumping and the drain stops draining. The fluid that arrives every night has nowhere to go. It pools. And because the skin there is paper-thin, it shows through as a shadow."

"Most women lose this slowly. About 1% a year after menopause. You'd barely notice for a decade."

"But some women experience sudden-onset drainage failure. The hormone shift is sharp, and two or three years' worth of that pump goes in a few months. That is your one winter. No birthday on earth works that fast."

"Your dermatologist is right that you're ageing. She's wrong about the cause of the speed. And she's wrong that the only door is a scalpel."

She pressed under my eye again. Four-second dent.

"The good news? Fluid is not fat. Nothing has been added to you and nothing needs removing. It has been parked. And unlike fat, it moves. The muscle isn't gone either. It's asleep. Not dead."

========

Then she said something that made the whole trip worth it — and made me sick all over again.

"You have maybe 24 months from onset where this fully reverses. Fluid that sits leaves a stain behind, and the stain sets. And a pump that hasn't worked in two years forgets how. After that, even good treatment can only hold the line."

She looked at me seriously. "You're at sixteen months. You have maybe eight months left in your window."

I had spent four of those months lying in bed until eight o'clock, giving up my mornings for a cause that was never guilty.

"What actually works?" I asked.

========

"Women who reversed this," she said, writing on the napkin, "did three things at once."

Move what's already pooled — the fluid sitting there will not leave on its own anymore. It has to be pushed along the channels, daily, until the channels open back up

Wake the pump — the ring of muscle has to be made to contract again, properly, on purpose. Massage moves fluid for a day. Only a working muscle keeps it moving

Clear the stain and rebuild the skin — the shadow left behind needs light at the right depth to break it up, and the papery skin has to thicken so it stops showing every shadow underneath

"All three simultaneously," she said, circling where they overlapped. "Creams sit on top of this. Surgery cuts around it. Massage only does the first one, which is why it must be repeated forever. This is drainage work."

When she said the second one — that the muscle could be made to contract again — I made her repeat it. After sixteen months of being told there was fat in there that only came out with a knife, I'd assumed there was nothing left under my eyes to work with.

I asked her what to buy. She smiled and said, "I don't sell anything, madame. Now you know what to look for. Most things do one of the three. Almost none do all three."

I folded the napkin into my handbag next to the receipt.

========

I flew home with an answer and a deadline.

Furious that I'd spent thirteen months and nearly three thousand on the surface — and four months of mornings — while the clock ran. Terrified because I had eight months left.

I started searching Facebook groups for women with sudden under-eye changes. Not slow ageing — sudden onset.

Patricia, 61: "Bags came on in five months, right when my periods stopped. Week eight, my dent test went from 4.1 seconds to 1.9. The half moons are fading."

Sandra, 57: "Sudden onset after menopause. Ten weeks in I went to work with no concealer for the first time in two years."

Michelle, 62: "My dermatologist said fat pads, surgery only. Three months in, I've got my eyes back. There's blue in them again."

They kept mentioning ReLumen.

========

I took out the napkin and checked it against Colette's three requirements:

✓ Move what's already pooled: microcurrent — a gentle pulse that walks the pooled fluid along the drainage channels instead of waiting on a pump that quit

✓ Wake the pump: the same microcurrent makes that ring of muscle contract, properly, hundreds of times in ten minutes. Read that again. It doesn't just drain you. It teaches the muscle to drain you.

✓ Clear the stain and rebuild the skin: 630nm red light — the wavelength that reaches the depth where the shadow actually sits, and where new collagen gets built

All three. In one device. Ten minutes a day. Exactly what Colette drew on that napkin in the café.

Most reviews were from women 55–68 who'd had a sudden change, not a slow one. Women in my exact situation.

They offered a 90-day refund, which meant I could try it without risking anything if my window had already closed.

I ordered that night.

========

It arrived in a small white case. Cordless, lighter than my phone. I used it at the kitchen window at 5:40 in the morning, in the dark, before anyone was up. Appropriate, I thought.

Ten minutes. Warm, with a faint tingle. Not sitting on the surface. Working where the fluid actually was.

Day five: dent test under my left eye, 3.4 seconds. Down from over four. Measurable.

Day twelve: I was rinsing a cup and caught my face in the window glass and the shadow looked... shallower. Like someone had turned a dimmer up half a notch.

Week two: the morning puffiness was gone by nine instead of hanging on until lunch. Dent test 2.9 seconds.

The fluid was moving. The pump was waking up.

========

Week three. This is the part I need you to picture.

It was a Tuesday, eleven in the morning, full daylight. The doorbell went. My neighbour, with a parcel the driver had left at her house.

My hand went for the hook. Four-second reflex, sixteen months old.

And then I stopped. And left the sunglasses on the hook. And answered my own front door with my whole face showing.

She didn't look at my eyes. She looked at the parcel. That's when I understood: the border I'd been defending for over a year had only ever had one guard.

Week five: dent test 2.2 seconds. The skin was filling back in like something was working underneath it again.

And one afternoon at the supermarket the young woman at the checkout asked how my day was going, and I looked straight at her while I answered. Straight at her. Not at the card machine.

I didn't just get my eyes back. I got back the part of me that looks people in the eye.

========

Ten weeks in, I emailed Colette. Timings and measurements, like a good student. Dent test: 1.9 seconds, down from over four. Morning puffiness gone by 7:30. No concealer since week six.

She wrote back: "The pump is working. The fluid is leaving. This is what reversal looks like."

Then she asked me for the name of it — to pass along to the women who come to her market table with eyes like mine.

I flew to France to get an answer from her. Now she sends women to me.

========

The woman at my book club — the one whose dark corner chair I'd spent a year trying to steal — started using it eight weeks ago. She'd been hiding the same thing for over a year. Turns out that armchair was her hook by the door.

Last week she texted: "I sat under the front window on Thursday. Nobody said a word. That's the whole point, isn't it. Nobody said a word."

Her dent test went from 4.4 seconds to 2.3 in eight weeks.

"Why didn't my dermatologist tell me this?" she asked.

Because dermatologists are trained in tissue. Skin, fat, and how to cut it. Not drainage. They see a shadow under a 59-year-old's eye and reach for the easy story: it's fat, it's your age, here's a quote. Mine gave me fourteen minutes and a four-figure estimate. A woman at a market table gave me an acquittal, for free.

========

If you're reading this because your face only exists in private now — if there's a pair of sunglasses or a corner chair or an angle you've learned to hold that has one job — if a doctor told you it was fat and your age and sent you home carrying it — understand this:

You're not ageing normally. And you almost certainly didn't do this to yourself. You're experiencing sudden-onset drainage failure.

Normal ageing = about 1% a year.
Sudden onset = two or three years' worth in a few months. No birthday works that fast.

And this is the part I need you to test before you do anything else. Fat does not dent. Press gently under your eye, hold for five seconds, let go and look. If a pale dent stays behind — even for a moment — that isn't fat. That's trapped fluid. And there is nothing under there to cut out.

They require completely different approaches.

Surgery removes tissue. Creams sit on the surface. You need drainage.

And no — you don't need to fly to France. I did that part for you. The answer fit on a napkin.

========

You have a window. In sudden-onset cases, that window is 18–24 months from onset.

The pump can still be woken. The stain hasn't set yet. But only while the muscle still remembers.

Every month you spend on the surface is another month of fluid sitting there, darkening skin that's already thin. Another season behind a pair of sunglasses and a four-second reflex.

I spent thirteen months and nearly three thousand on the wrong answers, and one week in France on the right one. The only part I regret is the thirteen months.

I don't want you to waste yours.

========

ReLumen does what Colette said was necessary for sudden-onset drainage failure:

✓ Moves the fluid that's already pooled (microcurrent, along the channels — not over them)
✓ Wakes the pump so it stays gone (that ring of muscle contracting again, hundreds of times in ten minutes)
✓ Clears the stain and rebuilds the thin skin (630nm red light, at the depth the shadow actually sits)

All three. Simultaneously. Ten minutes a day.

The only thing I found that matched all three requirements on that napkin.

========

Every day you wait is another day your window shrinks.

Every week is another week of fluid settling into skin that's already paper-thin.

Colette was clear: after 24 months, a stain is a stain and a pump that's forgotten how doesn't easily remember.

I almost learned that too late, in a country that wasn't my own.

Now you know. You have a window. It's still open.

But it won't stay open forever.

========

P.S. Ten weeks in. One payment, and it came with the eye cream. The flight to France cost more than eight of these. The fourteen-minute appointment that told me it was fat cost nearly twice what this did. The surgery she quoted was about eighty times it. Add that up.

The napkin is in my jewellery box. The receipt with Colette's name is under a magnet on my fridge.

And the sunglasses? They're still on the hook, actually. They're useful when the sun's low on the drive into town. But they're sunglasses now.

They used to be a wall.

P.P.S. My dermatologist saw me last month for a mole check. She looked at my face and said, "Whatever you're doing is working. You look rested."

I told her about Colette. About drainage failure. About the ring of muscle, the stain, and the window. About draining the fluid instead of cutting out a pocket that was never fat. I may have also mentioned, gently, that my sleep had an alibi.

She wrote it all down. Said she has other patients with sudden changes and nothing to offer them but a quote.

Sometimes medical training is ten years behind what a woman at a market table already knows.

This morning I had my coffee at the kitchen window at 5:40. Curtains open, face bare, sunglasses on the hook where they belong.
